transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-29
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Ana (Redwood Product), Emma (Nimbus CTO), Raj (ML Eng), Lina (Infra), Tom (Prod)

Summary:
Quick console tour of Optimize Launchpad for precision tuning; show INT8 vs FP8 profiles, demonstrate sandboxed tradeoff heatmaps, talk through latency and quality metrics, propose pilot next steps and security docs.

Topics:
- Sandbox/Launchpad overview
- Q-profiles (INT8/FP8/mixed)
- Latency vs quality heatmaps and thresholds
- Dedicated vs hosted behavior under tail latency
- Security & KMS / SOC2 concerns
- Pilot scope and benchmarks

[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run about 45 minutes of demo and leave time for Qs. Marcus and Ana will show the Optimize console. Emma, Raj, Lina — thanks for making time.

[00:22] Emma Chen: Thanks, yeah excited. We want to see how much we can compress without breaking clinical fidelity. Our product team is sensitive to hallucination risk.

[00:35] Marcus Li: Great, we'll start with the Launchpad landing page — you can see your tenant, sandbox projects, and a pre-run profile called "clinical-preserve" we ran on a handful of prompts.

[00:50] Raj Patel: Quick question before you dive in — our mean seq length is around 180 tokens but tail can go to 800 for long reports. Will that skew INT8 results?

[01:10] Marcus Li: Yup, excellent point. The console shows sequence-length buckets. For Launchpad we auto-suggest profile windows: low (0-256), mid (256-512), tail (512+). For INT8 we typically recommend a hybrid approach: INT8 on low/mid, FP8 or mixed in tail to keep KL/divergence low.

[01:42] Lina Morales: And what about KV cache persistence? We can't afford a re-warm every request.

[01:55] Ana Gomez: The runtime supports persistent KV caching per session for dedicated pools. The console's cost estimator factors cache hit rates — you'll see lower token cost when hits are high. Note: cache behavior depends on request affinity and our routing.

[02:20] Tom Brooks: Show us the heatmap you mentioned — how do you visualize quality vs latency?

[02:33] Marcus Li: Switching to the heatmap view... (screen) Here is a 2D heatmap: X axis is median latency, Y axis is quality delta relative to FP16 baseline (we use automated eval set + human-annotated holdouts). Colors show percent of prompts falling under an acceptability threshold. For Nimbus sample set, INT8 has median latency 32ms/token with a 1.4% drop in high-priority QA accuracy; FP8 is 38ms/token with 0.6% drop. Mixed profiles hit 34-36ms with 0.5-1% drop.

[03:20] Raj Patel: The numbers look good but can you surface worst-case tail latencies too? Our SLO is 99th percentile under 400ms.

[03:40] Marcus Li: Yes, on the right column we show p50/p90/p99. For a 16k context scenario p99 for INT8 spikes more — that's where fallback rules kick in. You can see a rollout policy we set: if p95 > 300ms, route tail requests to FP8 variant; if quality regression > 2% for a prompt cluster, fallback to FP16.

[04:05] Emma Chen: Who defines those clusters? Can we use our own test-suite?

[04:15] Ana Gomez: Absolutely. There's an evals tab to upload your test sets. Launchpad will compute regressions per prompt-id and tag. You can pin guardrails per tag — for example, all "diagnostics" prompts must be within 0.5% fidelity.

[04:40] Raj Patel: How reliable are the automated evals? We saw differences last time — sometimes the auto metric favors BLEU but clinical scoring is different.

[04:58] Marcus Li: We always recommend combining auto metrics with a small human-labeled holdout. The Launchpad UI surfaces both: auto-metrics, human-score concordance, and a divergence estimate. Where concordance is low, it flags for manual review.

[05:20] Lina Morales: Security question: the pilot needs KMS + customer-managed keys. Can we run private CP with KMS?

[05:32] Sofia Patel: Yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC peering. We'll share the SOC 2 and encryption docs after the call. For hosted pilot we can also support encrypted-at-rest model with envelope encryption and rotate keys.

[05:50] Emma Chen: Good. Also need audit logs that map tokens to request IDs (not user text) — we can't log PHI.

[06:05] Marcus Li: We have token-level cost traces but provide redaction hooks and PII filters. Logs can be configured to exclude payloads; we can provide only hashed request IDs for audits.

[06:25] Tom Brooks: Back to the tradeoffs — can you show a live A/B of INT8 vs FP8 on a couple of our prompts?

[06:38] Marcus Li: Yes. Switching to the sandbox runner, selecting two prompts from Nimbus's sample set. Running INT8 profile now... (slides typing) The INT8 response generated in 1.1s with slightly shorter enumerations; compare with FP8 which returned in 1.3s. Quality diff: human score delta -0.9 on that prompt.

[07:15] Raj Patel: Are those end-to-end times including network? How much of that is token emit vs compute?

[07:30] Marcus Li: Those wall times are from our sandbox in the same region — includes network and runtime. We also show breakdown: 60% decode/emit, 30% attention compute, 10% overhead. Under dedicated GPU pools the compute portion drops since we reduce overhead and improve batch sizing.

[07:58] Emma Chen: If we run a pilot on a dedicated pool, what commit size do you recommend for stable perf?

[08:12] Sofia Patel: Typical pilots for production validation are 2-4 reserved GPUs for 3 months depending on throughput. We'll size based on your qps and peak concurrency; Marcus will run an initial sizing with your distribution.

[08:30] Raj Patel: About quant sensitivity — how do you determine which layers to keep in FP8 vs INT8? Is that manual?

[08:45] Marcus Li: The Optimize tool has a layer-sensitivity analyzer. It runs per-layer perturbation tests and suggests a precision map: e.g., key/query matmuls to INT8, normalization layers to FP8. We show a recommended profile and you can accept, tweak, and re-run validation.

[09:12] Tom Brooks: Does that analyzer respect licensing for models? We have an internal constraint for some foundation models.

[09:25] Ana Gomez: It's agnostic — it operates on the model stored in your sandbox. If there are license restrictions, you can run the analyzer on-prem in Private deployment.

[09:40] Emma Chen: We need a clear rollback path if quality drops after rollout.

[09:50] Marcus Li: Rollouts in the Console support canary % by route, automatic rollback triggers on both latency and eval regressions, and on-call paging hooks. You can set a fast-fail rule: revert if any cluster exceeds 1% degradation for two consecutive runs.

[10:10] Raj Patel: What about cost math? How much cheaper is INT8 token cost vs FP8?

[10:20] Marcus Li: Our cost estimator shows unit cost delta based on kernel runtimes. On A100-style hardware INT8 can be 25-35% cheaper in pure compute. But end-to-end savings depend on cache hit rate and batching; we present a projected invoice delta. For Nimbus sample run, projected token cost reduced ~28% with mixed rollout.

[10:48] Lina Morales: And degradation risk? If we push INT8 across the board, how often does it require human rollback?

[11:00] Marcus Li: In our dataset of production pilots, broad INT8 rollouts had a manual intervention rate of ~7% across heterogeneous prompt sets. With guardrails and prompt-tagging that drops to ~2-3%.

[11:18] Emma Chen: Can we run a blind AB with internal raters? We don't want to bias them.

[11:28] Ana Gomez: Yes — the Eval module supports blind batches and aggregated scoring. You can set a human-rater pool and we can ingest their scores into Launchpad.

[11:40] Tom Brooks: Earlier you mentioned fallback policies. Can those be per-route? We have routes for "summarize" and "diagnosis" and different SLAs.

[11:52] Marcus Li: Per-route policies are supported. You can attach profile maps, fallback rules, and required thresholds per route. For example: Summarize -> aggressive batching + INT8; Diagnosis -> strict fidelity + FP8/FP16.

[12:10] Raj Patel: Performance under concurrency — will batching raise tail latencies for short requests?

[12:22] Marcus Li: Batching yields throughput wins but can increase latency for low-latency routes. Console suggests dynamic batching policies: min-batch and max-wait. You can opt for low-latency lanes with small batch sizes and higher unit cost.

[12:40] Emma Chen: Let's talk about the pilot timeline and success criteria.

[12:50] Sofia Patel: Proposed pilot: 8-week pilot, two dedicated GPUs, run ~100k sample requests/day drawn from your traffic window, evaluate quality with 5k human evals across critical prompt tags. Success criteria: p99 latency < 400ms, no >1% degradation on diagnosis tag, and >20% projected unit-cost savings.

[13:22] Emilio? (unintelligible): [murmur]

[13:28] Raj Patel: Does Redwood help tune profiles during the pilot?

[13:35] Marcus Li: Yes, SEs and Optimize tooling will iterate. We'll run weekly sweeps, update qprofiles, and keep a changelog with rollouts.

[13:50] Lina Morales: We'll need SAML SSO and RBAC before any private networking.

[13:58] Sofia Patel: Absolutely — we support SAML (IdP integration), granular RBAC, and audit trails for admin actions. We'll share integration guides.

[14:15] Tom Brooks: Any examples of health-care customers who've done this? Without naming specifics — high level, what went well?

[14:25] Ana Gomez: One payer customer reduced unit compute cost 31% while maintaining clinical fidelity by using mixed precision and per-route guardrails; the other big win was fewer manual rollbacks because they invested in a small human eval panel early.

[14:48] Emma Chen: Okay, let's close with immediate asks — Marcus, can you run the baseline with our sample set?

[14:58] Marcus Li: Yes, we just need the request distribution and the bucketed sequence lengths — Lina had said she'd share. We'll run INT8/FP8/mixed and return a report.

[15:10] Emma Chen: We'll get that over today. Also please include the SOC2 + KMS docs.

[15:20] Sofia Patel: We'll send sandbox invite and worksheet by tomorrow. Also attaching a sample pilot quote.

[15:28] Raj Patel: One last random: what about model variants? If the baseline model is open-source vs proprietary does that change answer?

[15:40] Marcus Li: It shifts the options: some closed models don't allow certain binary modifications; for open models we can run more aggressive layer remap. But from a runtime perspective profiles are model-specific, which Launchpad handles.

[15:58] Emma Chen: Thanks everyone. This was useful — we'll reconvene after you share the baseline.

Recap / Next steps (as discussed):
- Redwood: Share sandbox invite + benchmark worksheet (Sofia)
- Redwood SE: Run baseline INT8/FP8/mixed using Nimbus sample set, return heatmap & p99s (Marcus)
- Nimbus: Share request distribution and sample prompts, confirm pilot stakeholders (Lina / Emma)
- Redwood: Share security docs (SOC2, KMS integration, SAML guide)

End of meeting.
